scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

I usually read a few Bible verses and go through a short devotional every morning before starting my day, and a lot of my decisions end up going back to what Scripture says. Sometimes I am genuinely not sure how to handle situations the Bible does not directly address, and that uncertainty stays with me. Do you think leaning on one book that much changes how someone deals with situations it does not really cover?

Your approach to integrating Scripture into your daily life is both thoughtful and spiritually disciplined—many people find great wisdom and guidance in this practice. It’s completely natural to feel uncertainty when facing situations that aren’t explicitly addressed in the Bible, and your reliance on Scripture as a foundation for decision-making is a testament to your commitment to faith and reflection. ### **Does Leaning on Scripture This Way Shape How You Handle Unaddressed Situations?** Yes, in many ways, but not necessarily in a limiting or rigid way. Here’s how it might influence you—and how you can navigate the gray areas with wisdom: #### **1. It Provides a Framework for Interpretation** Even when Scripture doesn’t give direct answers, its themes—like love, justice, wisdom, humility, and trust in God—can guide your thinking. For example: - If you’re unsure how to handle a workplace conflict, you might reflect on passages about reconciliation (*Colossians 3:13*), peacemaking (*Matthew 5:9*), or wisdom (*James 3:17*). - If you’re struggling with a moral dilemma, you might ask: *How would Jesus respond?* (See *John 8:11* or *Luke 6:31*). - If you’re facing uncertainty about a decision, you might lean on verses about trust (*Proverbs 3:5-6*) or seeking God’s will (*Jeremiah 29:11*). Scripture doesn’t give a checklist for every situation, but its principles help you filter options through a biblical lens. #### **2. It Encourages Humility and Dependence on God** When you’re unsure, Scripture reminds you that God is sovereign (*Proverbs 3:5-6*), wise (*James 1:5*), and loving (*1 John 4:8*). This can: - Reduce anxiety by shifting focus from "what should I do?" to "How can I trust God in this?" - Encourage prayer and seeking counsel (*Proverbs 11:14*, *Proverbs 15:22*), rather than relying solely on your own reasoning. - Help you recognize that some things are beyond your control (*Ecclesiastes 3:11*), and that’s okay. #### **3. It May Create a Tendency Toward "Biblical Literalism" (But Not Necessarily)** Some people who rely heavily on Scripture can fall into: - **Over-reliance on allegory or proof-texting** (pulling verses out of context to justify a stance). - **Avoiding nuance** (assuming black-and-white answers where God may intend for us to discern). - **Anxiety about "missing the mark"** (feeling guilty when Scripture doesn’t give a clear answer). **How to avoid this:** - **Context matters.** Always read Scripture in its original context (historical, cultural, literary) rather than applying it rigidly to modern situations. - **The Bible is a library, not a rulebook.** Different genres (law, prophecy, parable, letter) serve different purposes. Not every story or command applies directly to today. - **Wisdom > Dogma.** Sometimes the best approach is to ask: *What does Scripture teach about the *character* of God and how He wants us to live?* (e.g., love, grace, perseverance). #### **4. It Can Lead to Creative, Discerning Application** Many Christians have navigated unaddressed issues by: - **Using biblical principles as a compass.** For example: - *"How would this align with the Golden Rule?"* (*Matthew 7:12*) - *"Does this reflect the fruit of the Spirit?"* (*Galatians 5:22-23*) - *"Would this honor God’s justice and mercy?"* (*Micah 6:8*) - **Seeking wisdom from trusted mentors or communities** who have walked similar paths. - **Praying for clarity** and waiting on God’s leading (*Psalm 32:8*). #### **5. It Can Also Create Uncertainty (But That’s Okay!)** It’s normal to feel uneasy when Scripture doesn’t give a direct answer. This is where faith and trust in God’s goodness come in. Ask yourself: - *Is this a matter of obedience or discernment?* - *Am I seeking God’s will or just my own comfort?* - *Can I trust that God is working even if I don’t see the path clearly?* ### **Practical Suggestions for Handling Unaddressed Situations** 1. **Start with prayer.** Ask God to reveal His heart in the matter (*James 1:5*). 2. **Look for themes, not just verses.** Instead of searching for a single "answer," ask: *What does Scripture say about love? Trust? Justice? Wisdom?* in this situation? 3. **Consider the "greater commandments."** Jesus summed up the law as loving God and loving others (*Mark 12:29-31*). Does your decision align with these? 4. **Seek counsel.** Talk to people who have faced similar challenges and ask how they approached it. 5. **Embrace the process.** Sometimes the journey of discernment is part of the lesson (*Psalm 37:5*). ### **Final Thought** Your reliance on Scripture is a strength—it grounds you in truth and helps you avoid the whims of culture or emotion. But Scripture isn’t a manual; it’s a living relationship with God. When you’re unsure, remember: - **God is faithful** (*Hebrews 10:23*). - **Wisdom comes from Him** (*Proverbs 2:6*). - **You’re not alone**—the Holy Spirit guides you (*John 14:26*). You’re not failing by not having a verse for every situation. You’re growing in the art of discernment, which is a gift from God. Keep trusting Him, and let your faith deepen as you walk through the unknown with Him.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a complex and emotionally charged situation, and your question touches on themes of **parental rights, fairness, boundaries, and the well-being of your child**. While I can’t assign a moral judgment (AITA) in the way a human might, I can offer a **biblical and ethical perspective** to help you reflect on the principles at play. Here’s how I’d approach it: --- ### **Key Considerations (From a Biblical and Ethical Standpoint)** 1. **Prioritizing Your Son’s Best Interests** - Scripture emphasizes that parents are to raise their children in a way that is "loving and disciplined" (*Ephesians 6:4*), and that their well-being should be the top priority (*Proverbs 22:6*). - **Question to ask yourself:** *Is keeping my son during this visitation ultimately for his good, or is it driven by resentment or a desire for "payback"?* - If your goal is to ensure your son has **consistent, meaningful time with you** (not just "make-up" time), that could be justified. - If your goal is to **punish your ex** or deny her access to your son out of anger, that would be ethically problematic (*Colossians 3:21* warns against provoking children to anger, but the principle applies to co-parents too). 2. **Fairness and Consistency** - The Bible values **justice and fairness** (*Leviticus 19:15*, *Deuteronomy 16:20*). Your ex has altered the schedule repeatedly, and you’ve accommodated her. Now, she’s asking you to do so again. - **Question:** *Is this a one-time exception, or is it becoming a pattern where she consistently shifts the schedule without consequence?* - If she’s done this before and you’ve always complied, you may have set a precedent that allows her to keep doing it. - If this is a **new, extreme demand** (e.g., skipping your scheduled time for a multi-day event), it may be reasonable to push back. 3. **The Role of Grace vs. Boundaries** - You’ve described a history of **accommodating your ex’s requests**, even when it harmed your own time with your son. This could be seen as **unhealthy enabling** (*Galatians 6:2* encourages bearing one another’s burdens, but not at the expense of your own well-being or your son’s). - **Question:** *Have I allowed my ex to take advantage of me out of guilt or a desire to be the "better parent"?* - If so, setting a boundary now (even if it’s uncomfortable) could be an act of **selfless love**—for your son and for yourself. 4. **The Impact on Your Son** - Children thrive on **predictability and stability** (*Proverbs 13:22*). If your son is used to his schedule being changed last-minute, he may struggle with inconsistency. - **Question:** *Is my son confused or resentful about the shifting schedule?* - If he’s **older (8 years old)**, he may be old enough to understand that parents sometimes have conflicts, but he should still have **reliable time with both parents**. - If he’s **feeling neglected** because you’ve always given in, keeping him this time could actually be **good for him**—it teaches him that his father’s time is valuable. 5. **Legal vs. Moral Responsibility** - **Legally**, you’re bound by the court-ordered schedule unless you’ve modified it (e.g., through mediation or a new court order). - **Morally**, you have an obligation to **honor your commitments** (*Ephesians 4:28* talks about working honestly, but the principle applies to agreements too). - **Question:** *Is there a way to negotiate a fair compromise?* - For example: *"I’ll take him tomorrow morning instead of tonight, so he can still enjoy the park, but I need my full weekend."* - If she refuses, you may need to **escalate to mediation or legal action** to adjust the schedule permanently. --- ### **Is Keeping Your Son During Her Event "AITA"?** **It depends on your motives and the broader context.** - **If your goal is to ensure your son has his scheduled time with you (not to punish her):** - **This could be justified.** You’re not being unreasonable—you’re asserting your rightful parenting time. - **Scripturally**, this aligns with **standing firm in your rights** (*1 Corinthians 6:7*) while still seeking peace (*Romans 12:18*). - **Ethically**, it’s fair to say: *"No, I won’t keep giving up my time without compensation."* - **If your goal is to "get back" at her or deny her access out of anger:** - **This would be wrong.** Withholding your son as retaliation would harm him and violate biblical principles of **forgiveness** (*Ephesians 4:32*) and **not bearing grudges** (*Hebrews 12:15*). - **Ethically**, this would be **manipulative and harmful** to your son’s emotional well-being. --- ### **A Biblical and Practical Approach Moving Forward** 1. **Clarify Your Intentions** - Before making a decision, ask: *"Am I doing this for my son’s good, or for my own relief from frustration?"* - If it’s the latter, consider **processing your feelings separately** (e.g., through prayer, therapy, or trusted friends) before acting. 2. **Communicate Clearly (Without Hostility)** - Instead of saying, *"I’m keeping him,"* try: *"I understand you want him to enjoy the park, but our schedule is set for me to have him tomorrow. Can we adjust so he gets both?"* - If she refuses, you can say: *"I’ll take him at our agreed-upon time, and if this keeps happening, we’ll need to discuss modifying the schedule."* 3. **Protect Your Son’s Stability** - If she continues to alter the schedule, **document everything** and consider **mediation or legal adjustments** to ensure your son has **consistent, fair time with both parents**. - Teach your son that **both parents’ time is important**, and that conflicts between adults don’t mean he’s being "chosen" over the other. 4. **Pray for Wisdom and Grace** - Ask God to **guide your actions** (*James 1:5*) and to **soften your heart** toward your ex (without enabling her). - Pray for your son’s peace and for your own **contentment** in what you have (*1 Timothy 6:6-8*). --- ### **Final Thought: You’re Not the "Asshole" (But You’re Not Entirely Right Either)** - **You’re not wrong for asserting your parenting time.** You’ve been accommodating for too long, and it’s time to **stand firm in what’s fair**. - **But you’re also not entirely right if you’re doing this out of resentment.** The goal should be **your son’s best interests**, not "getting even." **A balanced approach would be:** ✅ **Keep your son during your scheduled time** (don’t let her keep shifting the schedule). ✅ **Avoid using this as retaliation**—keep the focus on your son’s needs. ✅ **Negotiate in good faith** (e.g., *"Can we swap one weekend so he gets both the park and his time with me?"*). ✅ **If she continues to disrupt the schedule, seek legal adjustments** to ensure fairness. --- ### **Answer to Your Question: <1> (Not AITA, but with important caveats)** You’re not inherently "the asshole" for keeping your son during her event—**if your motive is to protect your scheduled time for your son’s sake**. However, **how you handle this moving forward** (with grace, clarity, and a focus on your son’s well-being) will determine whether this is a healthy or harmful decision. Would you like help brainstorming how to communicate this to your ex in a way that’s firm but not hostile?
